jack-minnicken-1880-11.A1: JACK Minnicken, colored, who voted the Democratic ticket at the late election, was set upon and mobbed off the grounds of a colored Can meeting a few days ago because he asserted his independence as a citizen by voting as he thought best for himself and country. At the same Campmeeting, Manny Robinson, a colored Democrat, was waited on by a committee of eight Radicals and ordered to leave the ground in two hours or be shot. His only offence was voting the Democratic ticket.

section-hand-columbia-1880-11.A2:
Two Murders.
L. Nov. 20. - A special
CINCINNATI, Nov. 20.—A special dispatch to the Commercial from Maysville, Ky., says: Cyrus Ewing yesterday met Reuben Gaunt, 8 miles from Maysville, and having an old grudge against him, immediately began an attack with a knife, cutting an artery. Gaunt bled to death. Both parties were colored. A special dispatch from Columbia, Tenn., to the Commercial says: Emanuel Johnson, a colored section hand on the Nashville and Decatur road, yesterday shot and killed his foreman, John Booth, white, because Booth had discharged him. Johnson, if caught, will be lynched.

B.EWS SUMMARY.

Emmanuel Johnson, a colored laborer on the Nashville and Decatur road, in Tennessee, on Friday, shot and killed his foreman, John Booth, by whom he had been discharged. At last accounts Johnson had eluded arrest. It was believed that if captured he would be lynched.

The funeral of John Lee Chapman, ex-Mayor of Baltimore, took place in that city, yesterday afternoon, from the Episcopal Church of the Ascension, on Lafayette Square. The Mayor and City Councilmen, several Government and State officials and many prominent citizens attended.

John Mehan was shot by William Engelskincher, in a quarrel in the latter's saloon, at Highland Falls, New York, on Saturday. Meehan died in two hours, and Engelskincher and his brother Jacob were arrested, the latter as accessory.

The unveiling of the statue of Alexander Hamilton, in Central Park, New York, was prevented by Saturday's storm. The President and Secretary Evarts, who went on to attend the unveiling, returned to Washington in the evening.

Michael Donly, a recently discharged soldier, shot and severely wounded a woman and then committed suicide in a house of ill repute, in St. Louis, on Saturday night. The woman had refused to marry him.

Frank Carr was shot dead by Frank Toliver in a saloon in Carbondale, Ohio, last Thursday night. There was no quarrel at the time of the shooting, but the men had a misunderstruding a few days before.

George Kraft, a Philadelphia, was seriously wounded last Friday afternoon by the careless handling of a fowling piece by John McCann, on the yacht Clara, in Chesapeake Bay, about fifteen miles from Baltimore.

Dr. John Townley, a well-known physician of Carbondale, Pa., was accidentally drowned, yesterday, by stepping from a plank crossing a reservoir. He was 65 years of age.

A. B. Meacham, the Ute Commissioner, arrived in Denver on Saturday night and was arrested as accessory to the murder of Young Jackson, killed by Utes in September last.

The schooner Falmouth, of Oswego, with a cargo of 16,000 bushels of wheat struck on the breakwater at Buffalo yesterday morning and sank. The cook, a woman, was drowned.

General Grant was on Saturday elected an honorary member of the Middle-sex Club, of Boston. The General was entertained by the Lotos Club, in New York, on Saturday evening.

Clara M. Guss, aged 46 years, was drowned in a bath-tub in West Chester Pa., on Saturday morning. It is supposed she was seized with an epileptic fit.
A young man, named McDonald, was shot through the heart in Ottawa, on Saturday, while scuffling with some friends and holding a loaded gun.

Vincenzo Staglia was fatally stabbed by Michael Barone, in a quarrel in a New York drinking saloon, on Saturday night.

Edward Nairn, a farmer of Napanee, Ont., was found murdered in his house on Saturday. His wife is suspected of the crime.

A brakeman, named Riley, slipped between some cars and had his head cut off, near New Newport, N. S., on Saturday.

John H. Oberly has been arrested for passing counterfeit $10 United States Treasury notes in Christian county, Ky.

Rev Daniel N. Dorsett died at Elgin Mill., on Saturday, at the age, as reported of 100 years, 4 months and 5 days. He was a native of England.

Charles Schaffer, age 21 years was dangerously, if not fatally, stabbed by Florian Gehringer, in a drunken quarrel, in Allentown, last evening.
Little damage was done by the recent frost in the sugar district of Louisiana, owing to the timely warning given by the signal Bureau.
section-hand-columbia-1880-11.A8: A lynching party has been organized at Columbia, Tenn., where a negro section hand shot a white foreman for discharging him.
section-hand-columbia-1880-11.A9:
News Boiled Down.
Dr. J. G. M. Ramsey, Tennessee's venerable historian, has resigned the Presidency of the State Historical Society, on account of feeble health.

A nephew of John C. Calhoun is insane, and labors under the hallucination that he is Jesus Christ. A wound received in the late war is the cause of his derangement.

The sentence of Lizzie Gass, white, to two years imprisonment in the penitentiary for marrying a negro was affirmed at the recent session of the Supreme Court at Knoxville.

Nashville, Chattanooga & St. Louis Railway stock advanced 54 cents in New York last Thursday and 8 cents on the day previous. Forty-one thousand shares were sold in the two days.

Fifteen Mormon converts passed through Nashville last week, en route to Salt Lake, Utah. They were to be joined at Huntingdon, Tenn., by sixty more. All were poor and ignorant people.

O'Neal's saw-mill, one mile west of Stevenson, on the Memphis & Charleston railroad, blew up Friday last, killing two white men and two negroes. Three other mill hands were badly injured—one fatally.

The Department of Agriculture reports the corn crop slightly below that of last year. There is a heavy decrease in tobacco and potatoes, although the area planted was about equal to that of last year.

The Alabama legislature, on Tuesday last, elected Hon. James L. Pugh United States Senator to fill the vacancy occasioned by the death of Senator Houston. The place is being temporarily filled by Hon. Luke Pryor, who was appointed by the governor.

It is said that Gen. Grant has lost heavily in recent mining speculations and that the property remaining to him barely yields him an income of $4,000 a year. A subscription for his benefit has been started and Victor Newcomb, late president of the Louisville & Nashville Railway, gave $5,000.

Hon. James E. Bailey, Hon. John M. Bright, Gov. Marks and Gen. W. B. Bate are prominent aspirants for the U. S. Senatorship. If, as it said, the low-tax men will not support Bailey and the state-credit members refuse to support Marks or Bate, the odds will be in favor of Bright, who is enthusiastically supported by the low tax and state-credit democrats of his own district.

The Minnesota Insane Asylum was destroyed by fire on the 17th inst. and 32 of its inmates were burned to death. The scenes during the fire were appalling and heartrending in the extreme. Numbers of the crazed patients refused to leave the building and ran about the halls and corridors screaming like Bedlamites. Some were half naked and in this condition rushed out into the bitter cold air and hid in alleys and dark corners. The building cost one million dollars and was ten years in course of erection. At the time of the fire it contained 656 patients.

Gov. James D. ("Blue Jeans") Williams, of Indiana, died Saturday last of inflammation of the bladder He was a plain, straightforward man, with but little capacity for public affairs; but the sterling traits of his character, especially his incorruptible integrity, made him exceedingly popular with the great mass of the people in Indiana. Men of his stamp, while they may not shine in high places, more than atone for any lack of lustre by the solid and substantial qualities of their character and the rugged honesty and fidelity with which they discharge a public trust.

John Booth, foreman of section 8, on the Nashville & Decatur division, was shot and almost instantly killed by a negro named Emmanuel Johnson last Thursday at Campbell's station, Maury county. Booth had discharged the negro from work on the road and thus incurred his ill will. The latter came to where the hands were working and after insulting Booth drew a pistol and shot him just above the heart before any one could interfere. The scoundrel was arrested and placed in the jail at Columbia. The people about Campbell's station are greatly excited over the murder and for awhile there was talk of going to Columbia and lynching the negro.

A man named Knox, one night last week, obtained lodgings with Mr. J. C. Hulsey, at Chattanooga. There was but one room in the house and Hulsey gave his guest, whom he was entertaining free of charge, the bed, while he and his wife occupied a pallet on the floor. About 12 o'clock at night, Hulsey awoke and found Knox standing over his wife, stealthily removing the covers and preparing to commit a nameless outrage. He seized the scoundrel and would have killed him if better counsel had not prevailed. As it was, he kicked him into the street in his night clothes, and the fellow wandered about in that condition until morning, when he was arrested. He pleaded somnambulism—said he was in the habit of walking in his sleep and was unconscious when he attempted to commit the outrage. He was formerly a Methodist preacher and has very respectable family connections in Marion county. He gave bail for $1,000 and was released.

william-jackson-hulcher-1880-11.A1: SHOT BY A POLICEMAN.—Last evening about 5 o'clock a negro named Joe Wills appropriated a pair of boots from a store on Broad street, and ran off. He was pursued and overtaken on Third street between Franklin and Grace. Officer Hulcher attempted to arrest him, and was assaulted by the negro with a large pocket-knife. Wills made every effort to evade arrest, and finally the officer was forced to drawn his pistol. Hulcher fired one shot at the negro, who all the while was trying to use his knife. The ball took effect in the ear of the left leg, making a painful flesh wound. He was carried to the Second police station in a wagon, and his wound was dressed by Dr. Brock. Wills has several aliases, and served a term in the chain-gang under the name of William Burwell. He is a noted thief, and has borne a desperate character.
william-jackson-hulcher-1880-11.A2:
POLICE COURT. The following cases were disposed of at the Police Court yesterday morning by Police-Justice D. C. Richardson:

Robert Owens, Elias Winston, Junius Lonax, and Cornelius Robertson (all colored), charged with assaulting and beating Charles Harris with a brick, and Cornelius Harris, George Lacy, Robert Owens, Ally Richardson, John Brown, and Elias Winston (all colored), charged with attempting to shoot Charles Harris. Robert Owens and John Brown were fined $2 each, and George Lacy $5 and Elias Winston $5 and cost.

Joseph Wills (colored), charged with stealing a pair of boots from C. W. Green; also charged with resisting and attempting to cut Policeman Hulcher while in the discharge of his duty. Continued until December 4th.

Lucy Hill (colored), charged with creating a disturbance in the house of Mrs. Carmody, was fined $10.
william-jackson-hulcher-1880-11.A3:
POLICE COURT.—The following cases were disposed of at the Police Court yesterday by Police-Justice D. C. Richardson:

Beverly Bryant and Ambrose Carter (both colored) were charged with stealing $15 from S. C. Graves. Bryant was discharged. The evidence was not sufficient to convict Carter, but he was committed for six months in default of surety.

D. C. Wulls and Mary Johnson (both colored) were found guilty of unlawful cohabitation, and were fined $50 each. They took an appeal from the Police Justice's decision.

William Jackson, the colored snatch-thief, who was shot by Policeman Hulcher a few days ago while resisting arrest, was tried, first, for stealing a pair of boots from C. W. Green; afterwards, for resisting and attempting to cut Policeman Hulcher while in the discharge of his official duties. For the first offence he was sentenced to receive twenty-five lashes. On the second charge he was sent on to the grand jury.
william-jackson-hulcher-1880-11.A4:
HUSTINGS COURT.—The following cases were disposed of yesterday:

Joseph Bailey, who was convicted in the Police Court of stealing $10 and a watch and chain, valued at $10, and sentenced to receive thirty-nine lashes, took an appeal to the Hustings Court, and was yesterday tried and acquitted.

D. C. Willis and Mary Johnson were fined $50 by the Police Court for unlawfully cohabiting together without being married. They took an appeal and were acquitted.

Jefferson Taylor alias Jefferson Jones, charged with breaking and entering the blacksmith-shop of W. B. Clarke with intent to commit larceny, was acquitted.

Joseph Wills alias William Jackson, charged with resisting Policeman Hulcher, pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to jail for thirty days and fined $10.

The grand jury will meet again Monday next at 11 o'clock.
